## interior_before_after

> Split-screen interior before/after edit; left panel preserves the original, right panel shows the renovation.

**Artifact:** `mockup`, `1920x1088`, aspect `16:9`
**Demo vars:** `templates/interior/_vars_examples/interior_before_after.yml`

### English

```
[1. Subject] A 16:9 split-screen before/after presentation of a kitchen renovation. The left half shows the room in its original "1990s oak cabinetry, beige tile, fluorescent ceiling" state, the right half shows the same room transformed into its "warm minimalist kitchen, oat plaster, smoked oak" finished state. A thin vertical divider runs down the centre of the frame.
[2. Action] This is an edit-mode pairing: change only the interior finishes, furnishings, and lighting on the right-hand panel; preserve the architectural shell — walls, windows, ceiling height, floor plan geometry — exactly as it appears on the left, leaving the rest of the room's bones unchanged. The viewer should read the key change at a glance.
[3. Scene] Indoor kitchen, identical camera position on both halves so the architectural shell aligns precisely across the divider. Light quality on each half matches the panel's era: subdued daylight on the left, warmer styled lighting on the right. No people, no pets, no exterior view of any real city.
[4. Composition] 16:9 frame split 50/50 by a 4-pixel hairline divider running floor to ceiling. Each half is captured at the same focal length, eye-level, centred on the same wall. Small "BEFORE" and "AFTER" labels sit at the top of their respective panels in small caps. A short single- line caption naming the key change runs across the bottom margin.
[5. Style] Editorial real-estate before/after aesthetic. Both halves are photoreal interiors; the after-half carries slightly warmer light and the refreshed material story. No HDR, no lens flare, no fish-eye, no artificial colour grading beyond what natural light implies.

Text to render exactly (chunked into named slots):
- before_label: "BEFORE — 1990s oak cabinetry, beige tile, fluorescent ceiling"
- after_label: "AFTER — warm minimalist kitchen, oat plaster, smoked oak"
- key_change: "Key change: cabinetry, lighting, and tile refresh; layout unchanged"

Preserve (edit mode only):
- architectural shell of the room (walls, windows, ceiling)
- floor plan geometry and ceiling height
- camera framing and focal length on the left panel

NO: human models, pets, identifiable real city views, photo-real real homes by name, lens flare, HDR oversaturation, rainbow gradients, watermarks, signatures, cartoon styling
```

## interior_material_board

> Square material / finish / color board (4-6 swatches with named labels) for an interior project.

**Artifact:** `infographic`, `1024x1024`, aspect `1:1`
**Demo vars:** `templates/interior/_vars_examples/interior_material_board.yml`

### English

```
[1. Subject] A 1:1 square material and finish board for the project labelled "Harbor Loft — Phase 02 Finishes". The board reads as a designer's deliverable: a grid of physical material chips (textile, wood, metal, stone, paint) photographed flat, each chip labelled with its material name and a short specifier note.
[2. Action] The viewer should be able to read the entire palette at a glance and pair each chip with its label. There is no styled vignette, no in- situ room context — only the chips themselves on a calm field. Tactile legibility comes first; nothing is decorative.
[3. Scene] Flat-lay studio surface — a soft warm grey paper field with subtle paper grain, even diffused overhead light. No props, no plants, no cropped hands. Chips read as physical materials, lifted slightly off the field with a quiet contact shadow.
[4. Composition] 1:1 frame. Top ~10% is a slim header band carrying the project label. The remaining ~80% is a 2x3 grid of six chips with even gutters; the bottom ~10% holds the palette keyword. Each chip occupies one cell, a small label tag pinned to its lower edge.
[5. Style] Designer-deliverable flat-lay aesthetic. Palette anchored on "warm neutrals, soft brass". Materials feel real and physical; metal chips catch a soft reflection, textile chips show weave grain, stone chips show veining. Geometric sans-serif label type, hairline 1px rules. No drop shadows beyond the chip contact, no glossy chrome, no rainbow.

Text to render exactly (chunked into named slots):
- project_label: "Harbor Loft — Phase 02 Finishes"
- material1_name: "01 — smoked oak veneer"
- material2_name: "02 — honed travertine"
- material3_name: "03 — brushed antique brass"

NO: in-situ room photography, human models, mood-board collage scraps, rainbow gradient, HDR oversaturation, lens flare, watermarks, signatures, clip-art textures, 3D extruded chips
```

## interior_room_mockup

> Photoreal single-room interior mockup (bedroom / living / kitchen) with one labelled accent zone.

**Artifact:** `mockup`, `1536x1024`, aspect `3:2`
**Demo vars:** `templates/interior/_vars_examples/interior_room_mockup.yml`

### English

```
[1. Subject] A photoreal interior mockup of a single living room styled in a "warm minimalism" idiom. The room is presented as a finished, unoccupied interior — one consistent volume, one camera, one read. A single hero object — a low oat-linen sofa with brass base — anchors the composition and is highlighted by a small in-frame accent label.
[2. Action] The image must read as a still interior photograph, not a lifestyle moment. There are no people, no pets, no spilled drinks, no implied activity. The eye lands on the hero object first, then surveys the room's volume, materials, and palette in calm order.
[3. Scene] Indoor living room interior at late-morning side window. Generic high-end residential setting; no recognisable real building, no view of a real city outside the window. Window light, where present, falls naturally on key surfaces; fills are soft and ambient rather than theatrical.
[4. Composition] Horizontal 3:2 frame, eye-level camera at roughly 1.55 m above the floor. Two-thirds of the frame are interior volume; one-third is the primary furnishing arrangement. The hero object sits near a rule-of- thirds intersection. A small caption tag in the lower margin identifies the room and the style keyword.
[5. Style] Photoreal architectural-interiors aesthetic — a quiet magazine-spread feel, not catalog gloss. Material palette anchored on ivory plaster, oat linen, smoked oak; surfaces read as physical (matte plaster, woven textile, real wood). Soft shadows, no HDR, no aggressive bloom, no fish-eye lens, no neon rim lighting.

Text to render exactly (chunked into named slots):
- room_label: "living room"
- style_keyword: "warm minimalism"

NO: human models, pets, photo-real real homes by name, identifiable real city views through windows, HDR oversaturation, lens flare, fish-eye distortion, rainbow gradients, watermarks, signatures, clip-art furniture
```
